sections.skill: Tell searching from generating, and explain retrieval-augmented generation

questions.domain: Everyday: searching and working with documents
questions.prompt: What does searching do?

choices.text: Finds existing sources and shows them
Retrains the model on the web

questions.correct_answer: Finds existing sources and shows them
questions.intro: SEARCHING finds existing sources, such as web pages, articles or documents, and shows them to you. GENERATING writes new text from learned patterns. Many tools now combine the two in RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG): the tool first RETRIEVES relevant passages (from the web, a company's files or your uploads), adds them to the context, and then GENERATES an answer based on them, often with citations. Retrieval can make answers more current and specific, but the answer is still generated, so it can misread or go beyond the retrieved text, and the retrieved sources themselves can be poor.

sections.skill: Compare a librarian with a storyteller

questions.domain: Everyday: searching and working with documents
questions.prompt: The librarian who hands you books is like what?
questions.correct_answer: Searching
questions.intro: A LIBRARIAN finds books and articles for you: you get the real sources and read them yourself. A STORYTELLER tells you a story from memory: engaging, but nothing to look up. Now imagine a librarian who first pulls three books, reads them quickly, and then tells you a summary in her own words with page numbers. That is like retrieval-augmented generation: helpful, but her summary could still mix things up, so you can check the pages she named.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Find where retrieval can go wrong

questions.domain: Everyday: searching and working with documents
questions.prompt: A RAG tool retrieved last year's policy instead of this year's. What went wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; last year's policy is always the same
The generation step invented a policy from nothing
The search step found an outdated version

questions.correct_answer: The search step found an outdated version
questions.intro: Retrieval adds new places for things to go wrong. The search step may find the wrong documents, an outdated version, or only part of what is needed. The generation step may blend retrieved facts with its own patterns or cite a source for a claim the source does not make. A search result page lets you judge sources directly; a RAG answer packages them for you, which is convenient but hides choices. When it matters, open the cited passages and confirm they say what the answer claims.
questions.feedback: Retrieval can pick the wrong version.
